Medicare at 65: Sharp RD Estimates

The effect of Medicare eligibility on healthcare use, with robustness checks

1 Specification

1.1 Estimand

We estimate the jump in healthcare use at age 65:

\[\tau_{RD}=\lim_{a\downarrow 65}E[Y_i\mid Age_i=a]-\lim_{a\uparrow 65}E[Y_i\mid Age_i=a].\]

Treatment is eligibility, \(1(Age_i\ge65)\), so \(\tau_{RD}\) is the intention-to-treat effect of becoming eligible for Medicare for people near 65. It is not the effect of being enrolled in Medicare; that is the fuzzy RD, reported separately. The main outcome is seeing a doctor in the past year (sawdr). An overnight hospital stay in the past year (inhosp) is secondary.

1.2 Estimator

Local linear regression within 5 years of 65, with separate age slopes on each side, survey-year fixed effects, NHIS survey weights and a triangular kernel. Standard errors are heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1). The specification is identical to the identification report; both use rd_functions.R.

\[Y_i=\alpha+\tau\,1(Age_i\ge65)+\beta(Age_i-65)+\delta\,1(Age_i\ge65)(Age_i-65)+\lambda_{year(i)}+\varepsilon_i,\qquad |Age_i-65|<5.\]

The sample is 69,622 respondents from NHIS 1992-1996, of whom 34,972 are within 5 years of 65.

1.3 What the identification report established

Age shows no heaping at 65. Sex, race/ethnicity, education and region are balanced at the cutoff, individually and as a combined index. Employment does not drop at 65, while the same test does detect the retirement drop at 62. Two features of the data matter here: the 65.00 age cell is only partly eligible, and both outcomes look back 12 months, so the effect should build up between 65 and 66. Sections 4 and 5 below address both.

2 Graphical evidence

Healthcare use around age 65. Points are survey-weighted quarter-age means; lines are local linear fits within five years of 65.

Each point is the share of respondents in one quarter-year age cell who saw a doctor (left) or had a hospital stay (right) in the past year. The blue line is fitted to ages below 65 and the orange line to ages 65 and above. The vertical gap between the lines at 65 is the estimated effect.

3 Main estimates

Specification Jump (pp) 95% CI (pp) p-value Rate below cutoff Relative change N
Saw a doctor (past year) 1.31 [-0.42, 3.04] 0.1379 83.7% 1.6% 34,972
Hospital stay (past year) 1.63 [0.06, 3.19] 0.0414 11.5% 14.2% 34,972

Doctor visits. Turning 65 raises the probability of having seen a doctor in the past year by 1.31 percentage points (95% CI [-0.42, 3.04]; p = 0.138). Just below 65, 83.7% of people saw a doctor, so this is a relative change of 1.6%. The confidence interval includes zero, so the jump is not statistically significant at 5%. Because 84% of people already saw a doctor before 65, there is limited room for this outcome to rise.

Hospital stays. The probability of an overnight hospital stay changes by 1.63 pp (95% CI [0.06, 3.19]; p = 0.0414), against 11.5% just below 65, a relative change of 14.2%. The jump is statistically significant at 5%.

4 Can retirement explain the jump?

The identification report found no employment drop at 65. To allow for a drop too small to detect, it computed the largest jump in each outcome that retirement could produce: the largest employment drop consistent with the employment confidence interval, multiplied by the gap in healthcare use between non-workers and workers aged 60-64.75. That gap overstates the causal effect of retirement, because people who stop working tend to be less healthy, so the bound is conservative.

Outcome Estimated jump (pp) Maximum retirement bias (pp) Bias as share of jump Jump net of maximum bias (pp)
Saw a doctor (past year) 1.31 0.07 5.5% 1.24
Hospital stay (past year) 1.63 0.08 5.2% 1.54

Retirement could account for at most 5.5% of the doctor-visit jump. Because the doctor-visit jump itself is not clearly different from zero, this comparison is less informative. For hospital stays the bound is 0.08 pp against an estimated jump of 1.63 pp.

5 Robustness of the estimates

These checks ask whether the jump is real, or a product of how it was estimated. In each table, a robust result keeps the same sign and roughly the same size as the main estimate.

Narrow windows compare people closer to 65 but use fewer observations, so they are noisier. Wide windows are more precise but rely more on the straight-line approximation.

A straight line on each side could mistake curvature in the age profile for a jump. A local quadratic allows for curvature, at the cost of precision with so few distinct age values.

5.3 Covariate adjustment

Adding sex, race/ethnicity, education and region should barely change the estimate if the groups on either side of 65 are comparable. Education is missing for some respondents, so both rows use the same reduced sample; any difference between them comes from the controls, not from the change in sample.

Saw a doctor (past year): Main: +/-5 years 1.31 [-0.42, 3.04] 0.1379 83.7% 1.6% 34,972

Saw a doctor (past year): Donut: drop 64.75-65.25 1.20 [-0.85, 3.25] 0.2513 84.0% 1.4% 32,166
Hospital stay (past year): Main: +/-5 years 1.63 [0.06, 3.19] 0.0414 11.5% 14.2% 34,972
Hospital stay (past year): Donut: drop 65.00 2.04 [0.35, 3.72] 0.0177 11.5% 17.8% 34,071
Hospital stay (past year): Donut: drop 64.75-65.25 1.22 [-0.66, 3.10] 0.2031 11.8% 10.4% 32,166
  • Drop 65.00. Respondents coded 65.00 were interviewed in their birth quarter, so about half had not yet turned 65. Including them as eligible pulls the jump towards zero, so dropping them should give a similar or slightly larger estimate.
  • Drop 64.75-65.25. If people postpone care until they are covered, use dips just before 65 and rebounds just after, which would inflate the jump. Dropping the cells around 65 removes this. The fit must then extrapolate across a 0.75-year gap, so the estimate is less precise.

5.5 Full exposure to eligibility

Both outcomes ask about the past 12 months. Someone aged 65.25 has had at most three months of eligibility within that window, so the jump measured at 65 understates the effect of a full year of eligibility. Dropping ages 65.00-65.75 makes the right-hand line start from people who were eligible for at least most of the recall window.

Specification Jump (pp) 95% CI (pp) p-value Rate below cutoff Relative change N
Saw a doctor (past year): Main: +/-5 years 1.31 [-0.42, 3.04] 0.1379 83.7% 1.6% 34,972
Saw a doctor (past year): Full exposure: drop 65.00-65.75 1.16 [-1.08, 3.39] 0.3106 83.7% 1.4% 31,335
Hospital stay (past year): Main: +/-5 years 1.63 [0.06, 3.19] 0.0414 11.5% 14.2% 34,972
Hospital stay (past year): Full exposure: drop 65.00-65.75 1.81 [-0.28, 3.89] 0.0896 11.5% 15.8% 31,335

If the effect builds up through the recall window, the full-exposure estimate should be larger than the main estimate. It is smaller for doctor visits (1.16 pp) and larger for hospital stays (1.81 pp). The confidence intervals are wide, so the data cannot distinguish a gradual build-up from an immediate effect; the dilution from the recall window remains a reason to read the main estimate as conservative rather than a finding.

5.6 Placebo cutoffs

If the method picks up noise or curvature, it would find “jumps” at ages where nothing changes. Each placebo uses a two-year window and data from one side of 65 only, so the real jump cannot leak in: cutoffs at 63 and 64 use ages up to 64.75; cutoffs at 66 and 67 use ages from 65.25.

Saw a doctor (past year): Placebo at 66 0.57 [-3.55, 4.69] 0.788 84.7% 0.7% 9,912
Saw a doctor (past year): Placebo at 67 0.57 [-2.08, 3.22] 0.673 86.0% 0.7% 13,386
Hospital stay (past year): Placebo at 63 1.55 [-0.86, 3.96] 0.207 10.0% 15.4% 13,520
Hospital stay (past year): Placebo at 64 -0.91 [-3.64, 1.81] 0.510 12.4% -7.4% 9,913
Hospital stay (past year): Placebo at 66 0.98 [-3.09, 5.05] 0.637 12.4% 7.9% 9,912
Hospital stay (past year): Placebo at 67 0.97 [-1.73, 3.67] 0.481 13.6% 7.1% 13,386

Two placebos have known reasons to fail that are not problems with the method. At 64, a significant drop would be evidence of people postponing care until they are eligible. Only four age cells lie between 64 and 64.75, so this placebo is also imprecise. At 66, the outcome rises steeply from 65 to 66 as the recall window fills with eligible months, then levels off. A straight line on each side can show that change of slope as a jump.

No placebo cutoff shows a significant jump for either outcome.

6 Is it Medicare? The subgroup test

The identification report estimated, for four race × education groups, how much Medicare coverage and employment jump at 65, and stated a prediction before seeing the outcome results. If Medicare drives the effect, the outcome jumps should be largest in the groups with the largest Medicare coverage jump. If the effect comes mainly from newly gaining insurance, they should follow the share uninsured before 65 instead. If retirement drove it, they would follow the employment jumps; but no group’s employment changed significantly at 65.

6.2 Which pattern do the outcomes follow?

The rank correlations below describe how closely the ordering of outcome jumps matches each measure, from -1 (reversed) to 1 (identical). With four groups they are descriptive, not tests. The formal test compares the two groups at either end of both rankings: white high-education and minority low-education people.

Outcome Rank corr. with Medicare jump Rank corr. with uninsured share Rank corr. with employment drop Minority low-ed minus white high-ed (pp) p-value
Saw a doctor (past year) -1.00 0.80 0.00 3.98 [-1.72, 9.69] 0.171
Hospital stay (past year) -0.40 0.20 -0.20 0.80 [-4.44, 6.04] 0.766

For doctor visits, the group pattern is closest to the uninsured ranking. The doctor-visit jump for minority low-education people is 3.98 pp larger than for white high-education people (p = 0.171). The difference between the two groups is not statistically significant, so the subgroup pattern is suggestive rather than conclusive. For hospital stays the pattern is closest to the uninsured ranking (difference 0.80 pp, p = 0.766). Neither outcome follows the employment pattern, which argues against retirement as the explanation.

7 Conclusion

Claim. Turning 65 raises the probability of having seen a doctor in the past year by 1.31 percentage points (95% CI [-0.42, 3.04]), from 83.7% just below 65, a 1.6% relative change, although this estimate is not statistically different from zero at 5%. This is the intention-to-treat effect of Medicare eligibility for people near 65. The effect on hospital stays is 1.63 pp (95% CI [0.06, 3.19]; p = 0.0414).

Robustness. Across bandwidths, functional form, covariates, donuts and the full-exposure check, the doctor-visit estimate keeps the same sign in every specification and is significant in 0 of 10.

Attribution to Medicare. The jump is attributable to Medicare to the extent that retirement is ruled out. Employment does not change at 65, retirement could explain at most 5.5% of the doctor-visit jump, and the subgroup pattern follows the uninsured ranking rather than employment.

7.1 Limitations

  • Approximate inference. Age takes few distinct values near 65, so HC1 confidence intervals do not fully account for misfit of the age trend within cells. Clustering by age cell is not used, because it performs poorly with this few cells (Kolesár and Rothe, 2018).
  • Attenuation from the recall window. The main estimate mixes partly and fully exposed respondents just above 65; the full-exposure estimate gives a sense of the larger effect of a full year of eligibility.
  • Local effect. The estimate applies to people around 65 in 1992-1996, not to all ages or later years.
  • Eligibility, not enrolment. The effect of actually having Medicare is the fuzzy RD, estimated separately.

7.2 References

Card, D., Dobkin, C. and Maestas, N. (2008). The Impact of Nearly Universal Insurance Coverage on Health Care Utilization: Evidence from Medicare. American Economic Review, 98(5), 2242-2258.

Kolesár, M. and Rothe, C. (2018). Inference in Regression Discontinuity Designs with a Discrete Running Variable. American Economic Review, 108(8), 2277-2304.
